# Use Alexa+ on Your Echo to Dictate a Voice Memo and Find It Again Later

> **In short:** With Alexa+ on an Echo, you can dictate a memo by asking, label it on the fly, and pull it back later by voice or topic — no phone typing required. Some Alexa+ features may require a paid plan, and your account must have Alexa+ active rather than the older classic Alexa.

By the end of this short guide, you'll have a small, reliable workflow for capturing an idea hands-free in one room and pulling it back out in another — without ever opening the notes app on your phone. If Alexa already handles your timers, lights, and music, this is the natural next step.

## Before you start
- An Echo (or any Alexa+ enabled device) already set up with your Amazon account, on the Wi-Fi you'll keep using.
- An active Alexa+ experience — Amazon says Alexa+ is rolling out to accounts gradually, so confirm it's on in your Alexa app.
- The Alexa app installed and signed in on your phone with the same Amazon account, for the management step later.
- Roughly ten minutes for the whole flow the first time; after that it takes about thirty seconds per memo.

## Step 1 — Dictate the memo in one spoken sentence
Stand within normal hearing range of the Echo and say the wake word ("Alexa"), followed by a single command that both opens the memo and says the content. The light ring (or bar) on most Echo models pulses blue while it listens, then changes color — usually cyan or white — while it processes. After a beat, Alexa speaks a short confirmation back to you. If your device has a screen, a small card may also slide in showing the captured text. If it looks different on your device, look for any pulsing or spinning light as the listening signal — the exact color varies by Echo generation.
💬 Example: say "Alexa, create a memo: call Mom about the dentist on Thursday."
You'll know it worked when Alexa confirms verbally that the memo was saved and the light returns to its idle state.

## Step 2 — Add a clear topic so the memo is findable later
Right after Alexa confirms, speak a follow-up sentence that attaches a topic label to what you just saved. You won't see a screen change because this is voice-only, but Alexa will repeat the topic and content back so you can verify it heard you right. The label is what makes retrieval by voice work later — without it, Alexa only knows the memo as "the most recent" one. If your Echo has a display and Alexa+ is fully active, a card with the topic may appear; otherwise, trust the spoken confirmation. If your device offers a different way to label, look for any "set a name" or "tag this" suggestion in the Alexa app — the exact wording changes between app versions.
💬 Example: say "Alexa, label that memo birthday party."
You'll know it worked when Alexa reads the topic and the memo content back together as one phrase.

## Step 3 — Confirm what Alexa+ actually captured
Within the same session, ask Alexa to read the most recent memo back to you. The light ring cycles while Alexa fetches it, then you hear the memo spoken aloud — your words, in your order, almost always. If the Echo has a screen, the text also shows up so you can read along. This is your safety net before you walk away: a typo in your spoken memo now is easier to fix than a typo you only discover next week. If it looks different on your end and Alexa reads something other than what you said, simply say "delete that memo" and try the original command from Step 1 again, more slowly.
💬 Example: say "Alexa, read back my last memo."
You'll know it worked when you hear the exact words you dictated, in the order you dictated them.

## Step 4 — Retrieve the memo later by voice and by topic
Come back hours or days later — from the same room or a different one with another Echo on the same account — and ask Alexa to find that memo by topic. The light pulses while it searches; if it finds a match, it reads the memo aloud. If your topic wasn't clear enough or you never labeled the memo in Step 2, Alexa+ may say it has no matching memo and you'll fall back to "my last memo" or "my most recent memo" — which only finds the very latest one, not older ones. That's why Step 2 mattered. If your account has the older classic Alexa instead of Alexa+, search by topic may not work and you'll only be able to read the most recent memo.
💬 Example: say "Alexa, find my memo about birthday party."
You'll know it worked when Alexa speaks the topic back and then reads the memo content without you repeating it.

## Step 5 — Browse, edit, and delete memos in the Alexa app
Open the Alexa app on your phone and look for a section related to notes, lists, or memos — Amazon calls this area different things in different app versions, so don't fixate on one exact label. Once you're there, you'll see a list of recent memos with timestamps and any topic labels you added. Tap any memo to read it in full, edit the wording, or delete it. This is also where you see memos you recorded on devices that don't have a screen, since the app is the single shared archive across all your Echos. If the section isn't where you expect, use the app's search or the More menu — it's usually near Lists, Routines, or Things to Try.
💬 Example: open the Alexa app, tap the menu icon (often labeled More or ☰), then look for Lists, Notes, or a similar section, and tap a memo to view or delete it.
You'll know it worked when you see the full memo text on your phone and can edit or remove it with one tap.

## Step 6 — Lock in a naming habit so retrieval stays reliable
Memos work best when the topic is short, specific, and said the same way each time. Pick a simple pattern — for example, project name, then the actual idea — and use it on every memo from now on. Over a few days you'll build a tidy, searchable archive instead of a pile of "unnamed" memos that all sound the same when you ask for them later. This step is a habit, not a feature, so the only UI you see is Alexa confirming each new topic as you go. If a memo gets a fuzzy topic like "stuff" or "ideas," expect fuzzy retrieval — Alexa+ will try, but it may pull the wrong one. Rename it in the app if that happens.
💬 Example: "Alexa, create a memo titled kitchen remodel: check tile prices at the store on Saturday."
You'll know it worked when, after a week, you can ask for any past memo by its topic and Alexa reads the right one back on the first try.

## Common mistakes
- **Skipping the topic label.** Saying "create a memo" without a topic leaves Alexa with only the most recent entry — fine for one note, useless for an archive. Fix: add a short topic in the same breath, as shown in Step 2.
- **Mumbling or trailing off mid-sentence.** Alexa+ usually cleans up small pauses, but long silences can end the memo early or drop words. Fix: speak in one smooth sentence, then ask Alexa to read it back (Step 3) before walking away.
- **Looking for memos in the wrong app section.** The exact label changes — Notes, Lists, Things to Try — so if you don't see them, search the app's settings instead of giving up. Fix: try the More menu, or use the in-app search box.

## What this means for you
- **In everyday life:** A spoken thought — a gift idea while washing dishes, a name a friend mentions, a task that pops into your head — gets captured in five seconds and finds its way back when you actually need it.
- **For your business or work:** A running "meeting prep" or "client follow-up" topic becomes a personal voice notebook you can query between meetings without breaking eye contact to type into a phone.
- **If you want to go further:** Try a small routine — for example, every Friday, ask "Alexa, read me all my memos from this week" and prune the ones you no longer need, so the archive stays small and searchable.

## Try it now
Walk over to your Echo, say "Alexa, create a memo titled test: this is my first Alexa+ memo," and then from your phone open the Alexa app and find it in the notes or lists section. The whole thing takes about thirty seconds — and you'll have the workflow ready for real ideas the moment they show up.
